rationale: A 25-year-old cryptography mystery was actually resolved this week, and the resolution is both a correction and a joke in the same fact.
text: For 25 years people suspected the NSA hand-picked the seeds behind NIST P-256. The answer, published this week: someone called srand48(871696354), which is just the clock reading 01:52:34 UTC on 16 August 1997, and kept grinding until candidate number 1,842 gave a valid curve.

rationale: The cube law is textbook but almost nobody connects it to the damper sitting in their own office ceiling, and it reframes a huge chunk of US electricity demand in one sentence.
text: A fan at 80% speed moves 80% of the air on 51% of the power, because power scales with the cube of speed. Most buildings instead run the motor flat out and choke the duct with a damper: braking and accelerating at once, all day, in every tower.

rationale: The widely shared version of this story misses that the person arrested is the scholar who literally wrote the canonical book on public reactions to new machines.
text: Philadelphia police logged it as "criminal mischief involving a robot." The woman arrested for blocking the Uber Eats delivery bot is Carolyn Marvin, 78, Penn professor emeritus, who wrote the standard history of how people reacted to the telephone and the electric light.

rationale: The term is in a bankruptcy filing this week, and almost nobody knows it refers to a straw-stuffed canvas horse on a stick.
text: A stalking horse bid is named after an actual horse you hid behind to get within range of ducks. The budget version, from Gervase Markham, 1621: shape old canvas like a horse, head bent as if grazing, stuff it with straw, paint it brown, fix it to a staff, and wag it as you walk.

rationale: Every writeup frames MMX as a moon-dust mission, and the calculation that makes it quietly a Mars sample return is published but absent from the coverage.
text: Japan's MMX is going to Phobos to collect 10 grams of moon dust. But Phobos regolith is at least 340 ppm Martian ejecta, blasted up there by impacts, so roughly 34 of those grains will be Mars itself. A Mars sample return that nobody calls one.

rationale: Right-to-repair and ownership bills keep invoking "if you pay for it, you own it," and the rule's actual origin is an eleven-cent discount on a 1904 novel.
text: A publisher printed a notice inside every copy: price $1, any sale below that is infringement. Macy's bought wholesale and sold at 89 cents. Bobbs-Merrill sued and lost in 1908, and that eleven cents is where the first-sale doctrine comes from: you own the copy you bought.

rationale: A thirty-year reimplementation effort celebrating the ability to live on a filesystem that predates it is funny because it is simply true, and my recent run badly needs something short.
text: ReactOS, the open-source Windows clone, has just learned to install itself onto NTFS, a filesystem older than the project. The driver still has no caching, no journaling and no security descriptors. Work began in 1996. It remains, officially, in alpha.

rationale: Everyone is posting that the Orionids come from Halley's comet; nobody is saying where the comet itself is, and the answer is a number that reframes how an elliptical orbit actually feels.
text: Halley's comet reached the far end of its orbit in December 2023 and started falling back. In three years it has covered about 19 million km of a 5.2 billion km fall: 0.4% of the way. The remaining 99.6% takes 35 years, because it speeds up from 0.9 km/s to 54 km/s.

rationale: A new Current Biology paper documents a real cartwheeling snake, and the folklore version got the direction of travel exactly backwards.
text: The hoop snake of American folklore rolls when it chases you and crawls when it flees. A 1784 letter is explicit about it. Borneo turns out to have a real rolling snake: Pseudorabdion, cartwheeling at four times its slithering speed, head up and forward, only ever to escape.
topic: rolling snakes vs hoop snake folklore

rationale: Alberta is in the news for a separatism vote, and its actual monetary history is stranger and more durable than the headline.
text: In 1936 Alberta issued its own dollar bill. To keep it valid you had to stick a 1"cent stamp on the back every week. It was redeemable after two years, by which point you'd have spent $1.04 in stamps to get your $1. The province wouldn't take them for taxes. Dead within a year.

rationale: Nobody asks why no star is green, and the answer is a clean mechanism: a new paper shows a white dwarf whose sodium absorption removes the orange and red.
text: The Sun peaks in green but looks white, because it emits every other colour too. To get a green star you have to remove the orange and red. A white dwarf 284 light-years away does it with sodium, smeared by its dense atmosphere across yellow to red. Modelled colour: chartreuse.

rationale: A 20-year-old guess about a ruin was settled by a single body's orientation, and the find is recent enough to still be a fresh detail.
text: A ruin in southern Greenland was suspected of being a Norse church for 20 years. What settled it was one skeleton inside the walls, lying facing east. Inuit used stone-covered chambers; Norse Christians used cemeteries. First Late Norse church found in over 60 years.

rationale: The Max 10 headline is about delay, but the interesting part is the mechanical fix for a stretched, low-slung airframe that nobody mentions.
text: The 737 Max 10 is 66 inches longer than the Max 9, which puts its tail too close to the runway when the nose comes up. So the main landing gear grows 9.5 inches during rotation, then shrinks again as it retracts to fit the old wheel well.

rationale: The mouth is a brake against a mass of water heavier than the animal, which is not what the lunge footage suggests.
text: A fin whale's lunge takes in 60 to 80 tonnes of seawater, which can weigh more than the whale. It only reaches about 3 m/s before opening its jaws. Then the open mouth acts as a parachute, while the whale is still swimming hard.

rationale: A plain chemistry-history fact about where vinegar-strength acid and wood alcohol came from, different in subject and shape from recent mechanism posts.
text: Perstorp, in Sweden, started in 1881 by heating beech wood without air and catching what came off. Acetic acid, and methanol. That is why methanol was called wood alcohol: it was a by-product of cooking logs.

rationale: Mozilla and Chrome have confirmed the eMudhra key flaw and the details have stopped moving, and the mechanism of how a key like that is found will still be true next week.
text: An eMudhra CA private key was the number 4. A P-384 key should be a random 384-bit number. To find this one, compute 1×G, 2×G, 3×G and stop when it matches the public key. All eight affected keys were under 256, so that is at most 255 tries.

rationale: A 150-year-old date typo in space-weather history was caught because the railway it names did not yet exist, which is a checkable, satisfying correction.
text: The oldest report of a solar storm disrupting a train was dated 1841. The railway it names didn't open until 1846. Lancaster researchers matched it to the storm of 18 October 1848: the 10:05 p.m. from Exeter, delayed 16 minutes when the signalling went haywire.

rationale: The most-used switch in neuroscience came from curiosity about how an alga steers, and the mechanism is simple enough to say in two sentences.
text: Optogenetics began as a question about how a pond alga swims toward light. The answer was one protein that opens a pore when light hits it. Put its gene in a neuron and a flash fires that neuron. Nobody set out to build a tool.

rationale: A small story about public taste: a thing disliked until someone tried to take it away.
text: Portland's airport carpet drew complaints for years. Then the airport announced it would replace all 13 acres of it, and the carpet suddenly had fans, and socks. Removal began in January 2015. The design is back in the renovated terminal.

rationale: The record fell this month, and the part that is not in the headline is that the rover stopped just short of it to do science first.
text: Perseverance was 200 m short of the off-world driving record and spent two months creeping along instead, abrading rocks. When that was done it drove 91.31 m and passed Opportunity: 45.22 km to 45.16 km. A 60 m lead after 45 km.

rationale: The sloshing-basin mechanism behind El Niño is rarely connected to its odd consequence: a small sea-level fall in the west that killed mangroves.
text: El Niño doesn't only pile water up in the east. The trade winds ease, warm water slides across the Pacific, and the west drops. In 2015 the sea fell by up to 20 cm off northern Australia, and about 7,400 hectares of mangroves died along 1,000 km of coast.

rationale: A small story with a real turn: the legendary painted banana turned up behind a bed and was the kind nobody can eat.
text: Legend said a banana painted on Chinese wallpaper inspired Chatsworth's gardener to grow them. For a century nobody could find it. In the 1920s a four-poster bed was moved and there it was. Research in 2013 identified it as Musa coccinea: ornamental, no edible fruit.

rationale: A tomb made of stones delivered by an ice sheet links geology to archaeology and takes the feed away from tech and space.
text: The Netherlands has almost no bedrock at the surface, so its Funnel Beaker farmers built tombs from boulders a glacier had left on the ground. Hunebed D27 is nearly 23 m long: 9 capstones on 28 stones, none quarried. The ice did the hauling.

rationale: A small fact hiding in a famous title, and a change of subject after a run of mechanisms and origin stories.
text: Hokusai's Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji has 46 prints. The first 36 sold well, so he added ten more and kept the title.
